Covers the chapter tip (principles/parts, principium, first-and-ultimate opening) plus densify through two discipline genera, right reason, God's revealing authority, divine revelation as first principle, Melanchthon on certainty from revelation, analytic method, and revelation's kinds, object, and modes (IV.7–XII immediate opening). Mediate continuation and the rest of Cap. 2 / the Syntagma remain.

source_text:
CAPUT SECUNDUM.
De S. Theologiae principiis, & quidem nominatim de complexo primo & ultimo.

I. Sunt autem in S. Theologia consideranda tum principia, e quibus illa arcessitur, tum partes in quas deducitur.

II. Principia S. Theologiae sunt propositiones a quibus sacra Christianae fidei dogmata per discursum sic deducuntur, deductaque in ea iterum resolvuntur, ut assensum hominis sani, modesti ac Deum timentis mereantur.

PRINCIPIUM in genere est id, a quo quicquam quoquo modo procedit; juxta Thomam 1. q. 33. art. 1. Est incomplexum aut complexum. Incomplexum est terminus simplex, idque vel principale, vel minus principale. Illud est ipse, vel, quod idem pollet, Christus, de quo 1. Cor. 1. Fulgentius lib. ad Thrasimundum pag. 108. Principium, ait, Christus, quia sempiternus praecedit: Finis Christus, quia perpetuus universa concludit. Principium Christus, quia ipse inchoavit: Finis Christus, quia perficit. Hoc est Verbum DEI, per quod Spiritus sanctus agit & operatur convertendo, illuminando, salvando homines, Rom. 1.16. 1. Cor. &c.

Utroque rite supposito, hic innuimus, primum principium complexum; quod est integra propositio, ex qua conclusio deducitur logice; unde & nonnullis principium logicum & cognitionis dicitur, quia ab hoc incipimus ea quae credimus logice deducere; ultra quod, ceu primum & generalissimum, in demonstratione non datur progressus. Hoc vero principium complectitur simul tum rationem quam qua est infallibile Dei testimonium, & rationem sub qua quae est revelationis lumen, eodemque sensu principium a quo & sub quo dicitur; ideoque longe aliter se habet, quam vel principium aliquod exterius, quod est occasionale nostrae fidei cognitionis & causa sine qua non, ut nobis hodie est auctoritas parentum, qui nobis veritatem salutiferam instillant, ut 2. Tim. 3.15. vel motorium, quod & ipsum topicum sive probabile argumentum est, ut miraculum.

Christiano his non opus est, quippe quae eliciunt assensum duntaxat humanae apprehensionis, fatente ipso Bellarmino. Quale igitur hoc nostrum est? Apodicticum & indemonstrabile, a seipso dignum fide, & cui nullo modo potest subesse falsum. Ad hoc principium adjungi debet causa sine qua non, nimirum auditio vel lectio, unde dicitur verbum auditus, 1. Thess. 2.13. Dogmata fidei exterius dico. Duo enim sunt dogmatum genera, alia ad credendum, alia ad sciendum. Illa sunt, quae speciali Dei revelatione nota sunt; haec quae ex rationis lumine patent. Illa creduntur, haec sciuntur. De illis hic proprie sermo est. Quae enim propositiones ad fidem proprie non pertinent, quales nonnullae in Bibliis occurrunt, eae huc non referuntur.
english: Chapter 2. On the principles of sacred theology, and specifically on the first and last complex principle.
I. Sacred theology asks us to weigh two things: the principles from which the discipline is drawn, and the parts into which it is divided.

II. By principles of sacred theology we mean those propositions that let us deduce the sacred dogmas of the Christian faith by ordered discourse — and then resolve the deduced dogmas back into the same propositions — so that a sound, modest, God-fearing person may rightly give assent.

Taken generally, a principle is whatever something proceeds from in any way (Thomas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 33, art. 1). Principles are either incomplex or complex. An incomplex principle is a simple term, either principal or less principal. The principal term is God himself — which is to say, Christ — of whom ([[1 Corinthians 1:30 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 1:30]]) speaks. Fulgentius writes to Thrasamund (p. 108): Christ is the beginning, for as everlasting he goes before; Christ is the end, for as perpetual he closes all things. Christ is the beginning, for he himself began; Christ is the end, for he perfects. The less principal term is the Word of God, the instrument through which the Holy Spirit converts, illuminates, and saves ([[Romans 1:16 >> Bible:Romans 1:16]]; compare 1 Corinthians and related places).

With those two incomplex principles in place, we turn to the first complex principle: a whole proposition from which a conclusion follows by logic. Some therefore call it a logical principle, or a principle of cognition, because our logical deduction of what we believe starts here, and demonstration cannot climb beyond this first and most general point. The complex principle holds together two respects at once — the respect from which, namely God's infallible testimony, and the respect under which, namely the light of revelation — and so is called a principle from which and under which. That sets it far apart from an exterior principle, which only occasions our knowledge of faith and is a necessary condition without which faith does not arise (today, for example, the parental authority that plants saving truth in us: [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]), and also far apart from a motive principle, which is only a topical or probable argument, such as a miracle.

A Christian does not depend on those lesser supports. They win only the assent of human apprehension — Bellarmine himself grants as much. What then is our principle? It is apodictic and indemonstrable, worthy of faith from itself, and such that falsehood cannot underlie it in any way. Still, a necessary condition must be joined to it — hearing or reading — which is why Scripture calls it the word of hearing ([[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]]). I am speaking of the dogmas of faith as they reach us from outside. Dogmas come in two kinds: some for believing, others for knowing. The first kind is known by God's special revelation; the second lies open under the light of reason. The first is believed; the second is known. Our subject here is properly the former. Propositions that do not properly belong to faith — and some such do appear in the Bible — fall outside this account.

source_text:
XI. Estque immediata aut mediata. Illa fere legatorum est, haec vero eorum ad quos legantur. Fere dico, quia aliquando etiam iis, qui non sunt legati, conceditur sui ipsorum informationem, ut Josepho Mat. 1. 20. & 2. 13. magis, ibidem v. 12.

XII. Immediata, qua Deus legatis suis verbum suum per arcanam inspirationem patefecit, eorumque ori imposuit aliis renunciandum.
english: XI. Revelation is also immediate or mediate. Immediate revelation belongs generally to the ambassadors; mediate, to those to whom they are sent. I say "generally," because sometimes even those who are not ambassadors receive it for their own instruction — as Joseph did ([[Matthew 1:20 >> Bible:Matthew 1:20]]; [[Matthew 2:13 >> Bible:Matthew 2:13]]; still more, [[Matthew 2:12 >> Bible:Matthew 2:12]]).
XII. Immediate revelation is that by which God disclosed his word to his ambassadors through secret inspiration and set it on their mouth to be announced to others.

source_text:
IX. Quantum ad modum, est revelatio divina declarans, aut probans.

Apostolus Heb. 1. 1. dicit πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως Deum olim locutum patribus, novissimis autem diebus istis locutum nobis esse in filio. Modi revelationum divinarum non exactissime sciri posse videntur, de quibus Petr. Galatinus lib. 2. de arcanis Cath. Ver. cap. 12. Paul. Fagius in paraph. Chald. ad Exod. 28. Drusius principio Comm. ad difficil. loca Genes.

X. Declarans, qua Dei voluntas nude significatur: probans vero, qua declarata veritas demonstratur.
english: IX. As to mode, divine revelation is either declaring or proving.

The Apostle says in [[Hebrews 1:1 >> Bible:Hebrews 1:1]] that God spoke πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως — in many portions and in many ways — to the fathers of old, and in these last days has spoken to us in the Son. The modes of divine revelation cannot, it seems, be known with exact precision. On them see Peter Galatinus, On the Secrets of Catholic Truth II.12; Paul Fagius in the Chaldean paraphrase on Exodus 28; and Drusius at the opening of his Commentary on difficult places in Genesis.
X. Declaring revelation is that by which God's will is signified nakedly. Proving revelation is that by which the truth once declared is demonstrated.

source_text: Etsi autem philosophia docet, dubitandum esse de his, quae non sunt sensu comperta, nec sunt principia, nec sunt demonstratione confirmata, ut hic licet dubitare, seu ἐπέχειν, an sola nobis cavitas sit causa, cur iris sit arcus; tamen doctrinam ecclesiae a Deo traditam sciamus certam & immutabilem esse, etiamsi nec sensu deprehenditur, nec nobiscum nata est, ut principia, nec demonstrationibus invenitur, sed causa certitudinis est REVELATIO DEI QUI EST VERAX. Verbum Dei facit nos ἀμεταπτώτους in fide Christiana πληροφορίᾳ, ut testantur tot martyrium supplicia. At analytica methodus applicata disciplinis, sive, ut clarius loquar, syllogismi didascalici, qui e propriis earum disciplinarum principiis deducuntur, efficiunt nos doctos in quoquo genere, in cognoscendo & assentiendo ἀμεταπτώτως, non ideo tantum, quia vim habent βιαστικήν, quae cogit & convincit τὸν ἔσω λόγον interiorem rationem seu mentem & conscientiam: sed etiam, quia ejusmodi syllogismorum rationes ex propria rerum subjectarum natura, non ex accidentibus aut aliis attributis communibus quibusdam, sed veris essentialibus, ducuntur. Ut n. aliis disciplinis nihil aliud analyticè propositum est, quam ut ex propositionibus vernaculis, quarum praedicatum cum subjectis habent essentialem & definitivum nexum, deducant nos necessario in cognitionem necessariae & vernaculae conclusionis: ita quoque in sacra Theologia nullus alius finis quaerendus est analyseos, quam ut beneficio logicae & imprimis analyticae accuratam nobis quaestionum theologicarum cognitionem ex propriis theologiae λήμμασι sumtionibus comparemus, & similes fructus percipiamus, ut sunt accuratae distinctiones propriarum & communium rationum, modus definiendi res spirituales, qui scilicet ab logicis praeceptis exspectari possunt; non etiam majores, ut est fides justificans, quae solius Dei munus est & a Spiritu sancto accenditur in cordibus nostris, itemque fructus fidei Spiritus sunt opera bona. Vide doctissimum Joachimum Camerarium in prolegomenis notationis figurarum sermonis in libros quatuor Euangeliorum, pag. 9. et 12.
english: Philosophy teaches that we should doubt what sense has not ascertained, what is not a principle, and what demonstration has not confirmed. So here one may doubt — or ἐπέχειν, withhold judgment — whether hollowness alone is why the rainbow is an arc. Yet we know that the church's doctrine, handed down by God, is certain and unchangeable, even when sense does not grasp it, even when it is not born with us as principles are, and even when demonstration does not find it. The cause of certainty is the REVELATION OF GOD WHO IS TRUTHFUL.
The Word of God makes us ἀμεταπτώτους — unshaken — in Christian faith with πληροφορία, full assurance, as so many martyrdoms testify.

The analytic method applied to the disciplines — or, more clearly, didactic syllogisms drawn from each discipline's own principles — makes us learned in every kind, knowing and assenting ἀμεταπτώτως. Not only because they have a βιαστικήν, compelling force that drives and convicts τὸν ἔσω λόγον, the inner reason, mind, and conscience, but also because such syllogisms draw their reasons from the proper nature of their subjects — not from accidents or from some common attributes, but from true essentials.

In other disciplines analysis aims at nothing else than this: from vernacular propositions whose predicates have an essential and defining bond with their subjects, it leads us necessarily into knowledge of a necessary and vernacular conclusion. So too in sacred theology the only end of analysis to seek is that, by the help of logic and especially of analytics, we may gain accurate knowledge of theological questions from theology's own λήμμασι — its proper assumptions — and enjoy similar fruits: accurate distinctions between proper and common reasons, and a way of defining spiritual things that logical precepts can supply.

Not the greater gifts, though. Justifying faith is God's alone to give, and the Holy Spirit kindles it in our hearts; likewise the fruits of the Spirit's faith are good works. See the most learned Joachim Camerarius, in the prolegomena to his notation of figures of speech on the four Gospels, pages 9 and 12.

source_text:
VI. Revelatio divina alia est generalis, quae fit a natura, Rom. 1. 19. alia specialis, quae supra naturam conceditur, Joh. 17. 6.

VII. Hujus considerandum est objectum & modus.
english: VI. Divine revelation is of two kinds. One is general, coming from nature ([[Romans 1:19 >> Bible:Romans 1:19]]). The other is special, granted above nature ([[John 17:6 >> Bible:John 17:6]]).
VII. Of this revelation, both the object and the mode must be considered.
